items.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010
items.q: He used to listen to Sonny Stitt, Gene Ammons, Stan Getz.

ctx.x: Well what, at the time, can you put into words what was the different approach, if you were more into Sonny than Trane? Less notes?

Less notes, more melody, more rhythm. I mean not that Trane didn’t play with rhythm, I don’t want to be quoted as saying that. But Sonny had a spontaneity. A melodic and rhythmic spontaneity I think compared to — Trane was more practiced. And even though, I mean it worked, you know don’t get me wrong, it’s not a put down by any means. It’s just what I was attracted to. It’s what I went towards. It’s what I like. You know you’ve got to be honest with yourself. And back in Youngstown prior to that, it’s what my…
And you got your rhythmic dose from that.
